en: Thus have I heard: the Aṅgulimāla Sutta, the eighty-sixth discourse of the Majjhima Nikāya.
At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Now at that time, in the realm of King Pasenadi of Kosala, there was a bandit named Aṅgulimāla, who was fierce, bloody-handed, devoted to killing and striking, and merciless toward living beings.
By him villages were made non-villages, market towns were made non-towns, and districts were made non-districts.
Thus, having killed man after man, he wore a garland of fingers.
Then the Blessed One, having dressed in the morning and taken his bowl and robe, entered Sāvatthī for alms.
Having walked for alms in Sāvatthī, after his meal, on his return from the alms round, he put away his lodging, took his bowl and robe, and set out on the road toward where the bandit Aṅgulimāla was.
Cowherds, shepherds, farmers, and travelers saw the Blessed One proceeding along the road toward where the bandit Aṅgulimāla was.
Having seen him, they said this to the Blessed One:
“Do not take this road, ascetic.”
"On this road, ascetic, there is a robber named Aṅgulimāla—cruel, bloody-handed, devoted to killing and striking, and merciless toward living beings.
By him villages have been made village-less, market towns made town-less, and districts made district-less.
Having repeatedly slain men, he wears a garland of their fingers."
"For even if ten men, twenty men, thirty men, forty men, or fifty men were to follow this path, O ascetic, practicing it repeatedly and together,
they too would fall into the hands of the bandit Aṅgulimāla.
When this was said, the Blessed One went on in silence.
A second time, the cowherds, shepherds, and farmers who were traveling along the road said this to the Blessed One:
"Do not take this path, ascetic; on this path, ascetic, there is a robber named Aṅgulimāla, a man of violence."
Lohitapāṇi was intent on killing after killing and devoid of compassion for living beings;
by him villages were made non-villages, market towns were made non-towns, and districts were made non-districts.
Having slaughtered people again and again, he wore a garland of their fingers.
"For even if ten men, twenty men, thirty men, forty men, or fifty men were to follow this path, O ascetic, following it one after another,
they too would fall into the hands of the robber Aṅgulimāla.
Then the Blessed One went on in silence.
The bandit Aṅgulimāla saw the Blessed One coming from afar.
Upon seeing him, this thought occurred to him:
"How wonderful, indeed! How marvelous, indeed!"
For ten men, twenty men, thirty men, forty men, or even fifty men might take this path together, repeatedly following it in a group,
yet they too would fall into my power;
and yet this ascetic comes alone, without a companion, as if by force.
"What if I were to deprive this ascetic of life?
Then the bandit Aṅgulimāla, taking up his sword and shield and fastening on his bow and quiver, pursued the Blessed One from behind.

Then the Blessed One performed such a feat of supernormal power that the bandit Aṅgulimāla, though running with all his might after the Blessed One who was walking at his natural pace, was unable to catch up with him.
Then it occurred to the bandit Aṅgulimāla:
“How wonderful, indeed! How marvelous, indeed!

For previously, I could run after and catch even a running elephant, I could run after and catch a running horse, I could run after and catch a running chariot, and I could run after and catch a running deer.”
"Moreover, even though I am walking with all my might, I cannot catch up to this ascetic as he walks at his ordinary pace.
Standing right there, he said this to the Blessed One:
"Stop, stop, ascetic!"
“I stand still, Aṅgulimāla; you too must stand still. Then it occurred to the bandit Aṅgulimāla:
“These ascetics, sons of the Sakyan, speak the truth and are true to their word.”
"But this ascetic, while walking himself, says:
'I am standing still, Aṅgulimāla; you too must stand.
What if I were to question this ascetic?"
Then the bandit Aṅgulimāla addressed the Blessed One in verse:
“You say ‘go,’ O ascetic, yet I am standing still;
you say of me who am standing that I am not standing.”
“I ask you this matter, ascetic:
how is it that you stand while I do not stand?
“I always stand, Aṅgulimāla.”
Having laid aside the rod toward all beings,
you yourself are unrestrained toward living creatures;
therefore, while I stand firm, you do not stand firm.
“After a long time, indeed, the Great Seer,
the speaker of truth, whom I have honored, has reached the Great Forest.
Therefore, having abandoned evil, I too shall wander forth.”
Having heard your verse connected with the Dhamma,
the robber thus cast his sword and weapon into a pit,
a precipice, and a hell.
The thief bowed at the feet of the Sugata and right there requested the going forth.
And the Buddha, the compassionate Great Seer—
To him who was the Teacher of the world together with its devas,
he then said, "Come, monk";
that indeed became his state of being a monk.
Then the Blessed One set out on a wandering tour toward Sāvatthī with the Venerable Aṅgulimāla as his attendant monk.
Wandering by stages, he eventually arrived at Sāvatthī.
There the Blessed One stayed at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Now at that time, a great crowd of people had gathered at the gate of King Pasenadi of Kosala’s inner palace, making a loud noise and a great clamor:
"Your Majesty, there is a bandit in your realm named Aṅgulimāla—cruel, bloody-handed, intent on killing and striking, and merciless toward living beings.
By him, villages have been made village-less, towns have been made town-less, and districts have been made district-less."
“Thus, having repeatedly killed men, he wears a garland of their fingers.
May Your Majesty forbid this.
Then King Pasenadi of Kosala departed from Sāvatthī during the middle of the day with about five hundred horses.
He entered the monastery.
Having gone by carriage as far as the ground would allow for a vehicle, he alighted from the carriage and approached the Blessed One on foot.
Having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. As the king was sitting there to one side...
The Blessed One said this to Pasenadi of Kosala:
“Great King, has King Seniya Bimbisāra of Magadha become angry with you, or the Licchavis of Vesālī, or other rival kings?
“Venerable sir, it is not that King Seniya Bimbisāra of Magadha has become angry with me, nor the Licchavis of Vesālī, nor any other rival kings.”
"Venerable sir, in my realm there is a bandit named Aṅgulimāla—cruel, with blood on his hands, devoted to killing and slaughter, and merciless toward living beings.
By him villages have been made village-less, market towns made town-less, and districts made district-less.
Having repeatedly slaughtered men, he wears a garland made of their fingers."
“Therefore, Bhante, I shall refuse him.
“But if you, Great King, were to see Aṅgulimāla— with his hair and beard shaved off, clothed in saffron robes,
having gone forth from the home life into homelessness— abstaining from taking life and abstaining from taking what is not given...”
“If someone were abstaining from false speech, eating only one meal a day, living a life of celibacy, virtuous, and of beautiful character—what would you do for such a person?

“We would pay homage to him, venerable sir, or rise up for him, or invite him to a seat, or we would invite him to robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick; or we would provide him with what is righteous.”
“Let us provide protection, defense, and guard for him.
But from where, venerable sir, could such restraint of virtue come to one who is immoral and of evil character?
At that time, the Venerable Aṅgulimāla was sitting not far from the Blessed One.
Then the Blessed One, having raised his right arm, said this to King Pasenadi of Kosala:
“This, great king, is Aṅgulimāla.
Then, indeed, fear arose in King Pasenadi of Kosala; terror arose, and his hair stood on end.
Then the Blessed One, perceiving that King Pasenadi of Kosala was afraid, agitated, and his hair standing on end, said this to King Pasenadi of Kosala:
“Do not be afraid, great king; you have no fear from this.
Then whatever fear, trepidation, or horripilation King Pasenadi of Kosala had subsided.
Then King Pasenadi of Kosala approached the Venerable Aṅgulimāla; having approached, he said this to the Venerable Aṅgulimāla:
"Is our noble sir, Bhante, Aṅgulimāla?
"Yes, Great King," he replied.
“What was the noble one’s father’s clan? What was his mother’s clan?
“His father, Great King, was of the Gagga clan; his mother was of the Mantāṇī clan.
“May the noble Gagga, son of Mantāṇī, take his pleasure here, venerable sir.”
“I shall make an effort on behalf of the venerable Gagga Mantāṇiputta regarding robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick.
Now at that time, the Venerable Aṅgulimāla was a forest-dweller, an alms-food eater, a wearer of rag-robes, and one who possessed only three robes.
Then the Venerable Aṅgulimāla said this to King Pasenadi of Kosala:
“Enough, Great King, my robe is complete.

Then King Pasenadi of Kosala approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, King Pasenadi of Kosala said this to the Blessed One:
“It is wonderful, Bhante! It is marvelous, Bhante!”
"To this extent, Bhante, the Blessed One is the tamer of the untamed, the pacifier of the unpeaceful, and the one who brings to final nirvana those who have not yet attained it.
For that which we were unable to tame with either staff or sword, Bhante, has been tamed by the Blessed One without staff and without sword.
Now, Bhante, we shall depart."
“We have many duties and much to do.
“Then, Great King, depart at whatever time you deem appropriate.
Thereupon, King Pasenadi of Kosala rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, circumambulated him with his right side toward him, and departed.
Then, in the morning, the Venerable Aṅgulimāla dressed himself, took his bowl and robe, and entered Sāvatthī for alms.
As the Venerable Aṅgulimāla was walking for alms on a continuous round through Sāvatthī, he saw a certain woman whose womb was distressed and whose fetus was perverted.
Having seen her, this thought occurred to him:
“Alas, sirs, beings are defiled!
Alas, sirs, beings are defiled!
Then the Venerable Aṅgulimāla, having walked for alms in Sāvatthī and returned from his almsround after his meal, [went to the Blessed One].
He approached the Blessed One, and having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side.
As he was sitting there, the Venerable Aṅgulimāla said this to the Blessed One:
"Just now, Bhante, in the morning, having dressed and taken my bowl and robe, I entered Sāvatthī for alms."
“Bhante, while walking for alms from house to house in Sāvatthī, I saw a certain woman with a miscarried fetus, her womb distressed.
Having seen her, this thought occurred to me:
‘Alas, beings are afflicted! Alas, beings are afflicted!’”
“In that case, Aṅgulimāla, go to where that woman is; having approached her, say this to her:
‘Sister, as far as I can remember since my birth, I do not recall ever intentionally depriving a living being of life. By this truth, may you be safe, and may your fetus be safe.
“Venerable sir, in that case, this would surely be a conscious lie for me.”
“Indeed, Bhante, I have intentionally deprived many living beings of their lives.
“In that case, Aṅgulimāla, go to where that woman is; having approached her, say this to her:
‘Sister, since I was born into the noble birth, I do not recall ever having intentionally deprived a living being of its life. By this truth, may you be safe, and may your fetus be safe.’”
“Yes, venerable sir,” the Venerable Aṅgulimāla replied to the Blessed One. He approached that woman and said to her:
“Sister, since I was born into the noble birth, I do not recall ever intentionally depriving a living being of life. By this truth, may you be safe, and may your fetus be safe.
Then that woman became safe, and her fetus became safe.
Then, dwelling alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and resolute, the Venerable Aṅgulimāla, in no long time,
realized for himself through direct knowledge and dwelt in that supreme goal of the holy life, for the sake of which sons of good family rightly go forth from the home life into homelessness.
“Birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being”—thus he directly knew.
And so the Venerable Aṅgulimāla became one of the arahants.
Then, in the morning, the Venerable Aṅgulimāla dressed, took his bowl and robe, and entered Sāvatthī for alms.
Now at that time, a clod of earth thrown by one person fell upon the body of the Venerable Aṅgulimāla;
a staff thrown by another fell upon the body of the Venerable Aṅgulimāla; and a pebble thrown by another fell upon the body of the Venerable Aṅgulimāla.
Then the Venerable Aṅgulimāla, with his head split open and blood flowing, his bowl shattered, and his outer robe torn apart, approached the Blessed One.
The Blessed One saw the Venerable Aṅgulimāla coming from afar;
having seen him, he said this to the Venerable Aṅgulimāla:
“Consent, brahmin, consent, brahmin! For that karma, brahmin,
by the ripening of which you would otherwise be cooked in hell for many years, many hundreds of years, many thousands of years—
even in this very life, you shall experience the ripening of that karma.”
“You have experienced the Dhamma.
Then, while the Venerable Aṅgulimāla was alone in seclusion, he experienced the bliss of liberation;
at that time, he uttered this inspired exclamation:
“He who, having previously been heedless,
later does not neglect himself,
illuminates this world like the moon freed from a cloud.”
Like the moon released from clouds,
one whose evil deed is covered over by a wholesome one—
He illuminates this world like the moon freed from clouds—
indeed, that young bhikkhu who...
He applies himself to the Buddha’s teaching;
he illuminates the world like the moon freed from clouds.
May people in every direction hear my discourse on the Dhamma;
may people in every direction apply themselves to the Buddha’s teaching;
may people in every direction devote themselves to me.
The virtuous teach only those things that lead to the Dhamma.
For all directions belong to me,
who speak of patience and praise non-violence.
Let them hear the Dhamma at the proper time,
and let them act accordingly;
for such a person shall never harm me.
Or whatever else there may be;
having attained supreme peace,
one should protect both the timid and the steadfast.
For irrigators lead the water,
fletchers bend the arrow,
and carpenters shape the wood.
The wise tame themselves;
some tame [others] with sticks,
with goads, and with whips.
Without staff or sword,
I am tamed by suchness;
"The Harmless One" is my name.
Having previously been a person who was harmful,
today I am truly named "Truthful," for I do not harm anything whatsoever.
"I was formerly a robber,
known as Aṅgulimāla;
I was being swept away by a great flood."
I have come for refuge to the Buddha.
Formerly, I was one with blood on my hands,
widely known as Aṅgulimāla.
Behold the going for refuge;
the conduit to existence has been uprooted.
Having performed such a deed,
Much leads to an unhappy destination;
touched by the ripening of karma,
I eat my food free from debt.
Fools of little intelligence devote themselves to negligence,
while the wise man devotes himself to heedfulness.
He guards it like the finest wealth.
Do not indulge in negligence;
do not cultivate intimacy with sensual pleasures.
For one who meditates with diligence attains vast happiness.
Welcome indeed, not departed—
This was not poorly conceived by me;
among all phenomena that have been analyzed,
I have attained that which is supreme.
It is well-arranged and not ill-considered;
this was not poorly devised by me.
The three knowledges have been attained.
Thus was the teaching of the Buddha spoken.
The sixth discourse, the Aṅgulimāla Sutta, is finished.
